title: Meaning in life and the misguided denial of death
subtitle: Transcendence of the self reduces death anxiety
author: Joshua Hicks
introduction: In his Pulitzer Prize-winning book, The Denial of Death, anthropologist Ernest Becker argues that most human action is taken to ignore or avoid the inevitability of death. However, psychologists Joshua Hicks and Yuhui Du argue that denying death is not the answer. Rather, increased awareness of death often increases meaning in life. Death makes life more coherent, purposeful, and significant, and by embracing death, we can be more ready to die with the knowledge that we will leave something meaningful behind.
body:
William James famously observed that “death is the worm at the core of human existence.” Despite our meaningful relationships, notable successes, and cherished pleasures, we remain aware that all of it will one day end, often sooner than we would like, and at a time we cannot predict. Although there is no escaping this insurmountable existential threat, we possess the psychological capacity to make the awareness of death more bearable, even transformative, by imbuing life with meaning.

Before examining why meaning may serve as an antidote to death, or at least to the anxiety it evokes, it is worth clarifying what “meaning” actually means. Most people have an intuitive sense of what it means for life to be meaningful, but in psychological research, meaning is typically viewed as a multifaceted construct composed of several distinct components or pathways.

When time feels limited, priorities often sharpen. People reevaluate values, repair neglected relationships, and revise the blueprint of their lives to better align with what truly matters.

First, a meaningful life is one that is coherent, that is, it makes sense and is comprehensible to the individual. Second, meaning often involves a sense of purpose, reflecting the presence of goals and direction that organize one’s actions and experiences. Third, a meaningful life is characterized by the feeling of significance, the belief that one’s life matters to both others and one’s self. Significance itself can take two forms: sociocultural significance, the sense that one’s life has value within a broader social or moral framework, and experiential significance, the felt sense that life experiences are inherently valuable and worth living. We next consider how each of these dimensions of meaning uniquely relates to the experience of death anxiety.

Coherence

For most people, coherence is not a struggle to attain. Life generally makes sense. If it didn’t, we would feel as bewildered as Alice tumbling down the rabbit hole. From an early age, humans need to make sense of their environment in order to survive, and that basic capacity continues to develop throughout life. Early on, we adopt general beliefs such as the world is good or good things happen to good people. As we mature, this sense of coherence becomes further crystallized through the development of a stable personal identity, which helps us move through life in seemingly predictable, manageable patterns. In this way, coherence may keep thoughts of death from surfacing too often or too vividly by keeping us plugged into the “matrix” of life.

Unfortunately, certain life events, such as trauma, loss, or other major life disruptions, can shatter this sense of order. The awareness of death represents one of the most powerful examples of these types of disruptions, whether through a cancer diagnosis, a sudden accident, or the painful loss of someone we love. When life feels like it no longer makes sense, we experience a kind of existential disorientation. Such crises often coincide with a breakdown in coherence, and, with it, a profound loss of meaning.

Yet the confrontation with death does not always undermine one’s sense of coherence forever. Paradoxically, it can also prompt a renewed and more fortified reconstruction of meaning. Many philosophers and psychologists have noted that the awareness of mortality can help spur a fresh sense of understanding. When time feels limited, priorities often sharpen. People reevaluate values, repair neglected relationships, and revise the blueprint of their lives to better align with what truly matters. In this way, death awareness, though deeply unsettling, can also serve as a catalyst for restoring coherence and reorienting the self toward meaning.

Purpose

If coherence represents the cognitive component of meaning, purpose reflects its motivational dimension. Purpose concerns what we aspire to achieve in life; it is what gets us up in the morning, motivates us to study and work hard, and provides extra fuel during these efforts. Purpose often consists of valued long-term goals that connect the present self to future possibilities, offering a sense of coherence, significance, and stability in life. Purpose also plays a role in managing existential concerns. Death, of course, marks the termination of all our terrestrial strivings. In response, scholars have argued that humans have developed psychological and cultural defenses to deny or transcend this fearsome inevitability. In The Denial of Death, cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker proposed that people create “immortality projects,” or efforts to achieve a symbolic form of immortality by committing themselves to pursuits that transcend mortal limitations. These projects often take the form of culturally valued endeavors, such as religious devotion, creative or scientific achievement, accumulation of wealth or power, close interpersonal bonds, or identification with enduring groups, nations, or causes. Such commitments provide a sense of “heroism” that helps mitigate death anxiety.

One might die, but the belief that one’s contributions will live on provides a sense of symbolic permanence.

From this perspective, because life purposes are often anchored in culturally significant values and ideals, having a clear sense of purpose affirms progress toward symbolic immortality. In other words, by working hard to provide for one’s family, advancing knowledge, or contributing to one’s community, individuals enact culturally recognized forms of heroism, allowing their efforts and creations to outlive their physical existence. In contrast, the absence of purpose may evoke feelings of aimlessness, signaling a perceived failure or inability to achieve symbolic transcendence. Such experiences can elicit heightened death anxiety, as the individual is left without a sense of enduring meaning or legacy.

Significance

While coherence and purpose may have associations with death anxiety, the feeling of significance has perhaps a more robust relationship to it. In particular, sociomoral significance, the sense that one’s life matters to others and contributes to something larger than oneself, has long been viewed as a buffer against death anxiety. As mentioned, the writings of Ernest Becker, as well as Irvin Yalom and many others, emphasize that feeling significant mitigates existential fear. From a psychological standpoint, Terror Management Theory (TMT) is especially relevant. According to TMT, perceiving one’s life as possessing enduring significance, whether through close relationships, personal accomplishments, or cultural contributions, is what truly helps individuals symbolically transcend mortality. One might die, but the belief that one’s contributions will live on provides a sense of symbolic permanence. As Yalom (1980) observed, “The fear of death is always there, but it recedes into the background when life feels meaningful and significant.” Thus, both individual achievements and participation in larger collective endeavors serve as vital means of sustaining a sense of existential significance.

Feeling that life is significant arises not only from sociocultural sources but also from personal experience. At first glance, experiential significance, the felt sense that one’s life experiences are intrinsically valuable and worth living, might seem to heighten death anxiety. After all, who wishes to leave a world so full of beauty and joy? Yet experiential significance is also profoundly self-transcendent in nature. It is often felt in moments when the boundaries of the self feel like they have dissolved into something larger, such as nature, art, love, experiences of awe and wonder, or a sense of shared humanity. When people feel part of something greater than themselves, this awareness can likewise buffer against existential fear. In this way, both sociocultural and experiential forms of significance serve as distinct yet complementary routes to reducing death anxiety.

Although the awareness of mortality can disrupt coherence, threaten purpose, and diminish one’s sense of significance, it can also rekindle an appreciation for existence itself. Awareness of death often motivates people to make sense of their lives, to reprioritize what truly matters, to pursue goals that transcend the self, and to find value even in the ordinary moments of daily life. Meaning, therefore, serves not only as a psychological defense against existential fear but also as a profound affirmation of life’s worth. Through meaning, we transform mortality from a source of paralysis into a call to engagement. Indeed, for those able to shift their focus from what will be lost to what endures within the larger context of time and space, even the “worm at the core” may feel strangely sacred.
